decks.title: Quality Management
decks.subtitle: From inspection to institution · Session 11
decks.overview: Quality is multi-dimensional, so strategy means choosing which dimensions to win on. Most problems sit in the system, not the person. Prevention is cheaper than failure, and culture, not toolkits, is what competitors cannot copy. The deck runs in six moves: what quality is → the thinkers and variation → the economics of quality → toolkits → cases → synthesis.

sections.title: What is quality? Garvin’s lenses and dimensions
points: **Five lenses (Garvin, 1984, Sloan Management Review):** **Transcendent**: innate excellence, “I know it when I see it” (Taj Mahal Palace). **Product-based**: a measurable amount of an attribute, more is better (thread count, megapixels). **User-based**: fitness for use for this customer (Alto for a first-time city buyer). **Manufacturing-based**: conformance to requirements, right first time (Six Sigma, zero defects). **Value-based**: performance at an acceptable price (Jio, IndiGo).
**Eight dimensions (Garvin, 1987, HBR):** Performance, Features, Reliability, Conformance, Durability, Serviceability, Aesthetics, Perceived quality.
Slide title: **“compete on a few, not all”**. A firm picks the dimensions it will win on and may deliberately sacrifice others.
Warm-up pairs (Alto vs S-Class, ₹15 chai vs ₹350 latte, ₹9,000 vs ₹1,50,000 phone) show that people judge quality through different lenses.

sections.tip: Trap: Six Sigma / zero defects = **manufacturing-based**, not value-based. “Made in Japan” = **perceived quality**, not aesthetics. Lenses = 1984 SMR; dimensions = 1987 HBR.

sections.title: The 99.9% trap: scale changes everything
points: **UPI:** ~698 million transactions/day (21.63 bn in Dec 2025). At 99.9% → **~6.98 lakh failed payments a day**. At Six Sigma (3.4 per million) → **~2,400**.
**Mumbai dabbawalas:** ~130,000 lunches/day. At 99.9% → **~130** wrong or missed. At Six Sigma → **< 1 (≈0.44)**.
Lesson: a percentage that sounds high can still mean a crisis at national scale (“99.9% is a crisis at 700 million transactions a day”). The arithmetic is illustrative.
sections.tip: 0.1% of 698 million is **6.98 lakh**, not 69.8 lakh. Watch the powers of ten.

sections.title: A century of quality and the seven gurus
points: **1920s** Inspection & SQC: Shewhart’s control chart at Bell Labs (1924). **1950s** Japan learns QC: Deming (1950) and Juran (1954) lecture to JUSE; Deming Prize (1951); Feigenbaum’s Total Quality Control.
**1960s–70s** Quality circles: Ishikawa’s 7 tools; Crosby’s *Quality Is Free* (1979). **1980s** TQM in the West: Baldrige and ISO 9000 (both 1987).
**1986–2000s** Six Sigma (Motorola 1986, GE 1995); TPS becomes “Lean” (Womack et al., 1990); CMM/CMMI. **2010s–now** Digital quality: DevOps, SRE error budgets, continuous testing, AI-assisted code.

sections.tip: Fitness for use = **Juran** (and the user-based lens). Conformance to requirements = **Crosby**. Pareto = Juran; fishbone = Ishikawa; loss function = Taguchi.

sections.title: Variation: signal or noise?
points: **Common cause:** inherent in the system, random, many small sources; points stay within the limits → **fix the system (management’s job)**.
**Special cause:** assignable (a bank’s server went down on Day 14); the point breaks the UCL → **investigate and remove the specific cause**.
**Tampering:** reacting to every wiggle as if it were special **makes variation worse** (Deming’s funnel experiment).
Control limits at **±3σ** around the mean (Shewhart, 1931). Example chart: a fintech app’s daily failed-payment %.
sections.tip: Synthesis idea 2: “Fix the system, not the person.” Most variation is common cause, and blame is usually tampering.

sections.title: Service quality: SERVQUAL and the Gap Model
sections.topic: Service Quality (SERVQUAL and the Gap Model)
points: **PZB** = A. Parasuraman, Valerie Zeithaml, Leonard Berry.
Perceived service quality = **expected service vs perceived service**. Expectations are shaped by **word of mouth, personal needs and past experience**.
**10 determinants:** Access, Communication, Competence, Courtesy, Credibility, Reliability, Responsiveness, Security, Tangibles, Understanding/knowing the customer.

**Gap Model (Parasuraman et al., 1985):** Gap 1 expected service ↔ management perceptions · Gap 2 management perceptions ↔ service-quality specifications · Gap 3 specifications ↔ service delivery · Gap 4 service delivery ↔ external communications · **Gap 5 expected ↔ perceived service** (the customer gap).

**Linkages:** superior quality → favourable intentions → customers **remain** (+$: ongoing revenue, increased spending, price premium, referred customers). Inferior quality → unfavourable intentions → customers **defect** (−$: decreased spending, lost customers, costs to attract new customers).

table.caption: Key SERVQUAL definitions
head: Determinant
Definition
rows: Willingness or readiness to provide service
Freedom from danger, risk or doubt

sections.tip: Reliability is the only label in BOTH Garvin’s eight dimensions and the SERVQUAL ten. Referred customers is a **+$** outcome.

sections.title: Economics of quality: cost of quality
points: Crosby: “Quality is free. It’s not a gift, but it is free.”

**Cost of good quality:** **Prevention** stops defects being created (process design, FMEA, training, poka-yoke; IT: coding standards, threat modelling) and **Appraisal** finds them before the customer does (inspection, audits, lab tests; IT: code review, test automation, UAT).

**Cost of poor quality** (Crosby’s *price of non-conformance*): **Internal failure**, caught inside the firm (scrap, rework, downtime; IT: bug fixes before release, failed builds), and **External failure**, reaching the customer (recalls, warranty, lost customers, fines; IT: outages, SLA penalties, breach costs, churn).
**1-10-100 heuristic:** ₹1 to prevent, ₹10 to catch internally, ₹100 once the customer finds it (Labovitz & Chang, 1992). It is a heuristic, not a law.
Immature organisations spend heavily on appraisal and failure and thinly on prevention. **Mature ones shift the mix left.**

sections.tip: A bug found in **UAT before go-live** is **internal** failure, not external. Code review is **appraisal**, not prevention.

sections.title: Does quality pay? The evidence
points: **PAYS: Hendricks & Singhal (1997)**, ~600 award winners vs matched controls over 10 years: operating income growth **mean 107 / median 48**, sales growth **mean 64 / median 24** (% points higher).

**PAYS: Levine & Toffel (2010)**, ISO 9001 adopters in ~1,000 California firms: far lower death rates and faster growth in sales, jobs and pay. **Harter et al. (2000)**: higher software process maturity → higher quality. **Swink & Jacobs (2012)**: Six Sigma → ROA gains via lower indirect costs.

**BUT: Powell (1995)**: tools don’t create advantage; tacit culture, empowerment and executive commitment do. **Benner & Tushman (2003)**: process management can crowd out exploration and radical innovation.
Caution: a 2006 Fortune analysis found **91% of 58** large firms announcing Six Sigma trailed the S&P 500. Announcing is not building a capability.

sections.title: Toolkits: TQM, Lean/TPS, Six Sigma
points: **TQM, six principles:** customer focus, **leadership commitment**, **employee empowerment**, process thinking (y = f(x)), continuous improvement (kaizen), fact-based decisions. Powell: the tacit, hard-to-imitate core (culture, empowerment, commitment) is where TQM succeeds or fails.

**Lean/TPS:** **Jidoka & andon** (anyone can stop the line; build quality in), **just-in-time** (low inventory exposes problems), **kaizen**, **poka-yoke** (Shingo: design so the error cannot happen).

**Ohno’s 7 wastes for IT:** Transport → hand-offs · Inventory → unreleased code / WIP · Motion → context switching · Waiting → approvals, environments · Overproduction → unused features · Over-processing → gold-plating, extra sign-offs · Defects → bugs, rework, incidents.

**Six Sigma DMAIC:** **Define** (problem, CTQs, scope) → **Measure** (baseline, sigma) → **Analyze** (root causes, y = f(x)) → **Improve** (pilot, implement) → **Control** (control plans, SPC). Motorola / Bill Smith (1986); GE / Jack Welch (1995).
sections.tip: Context switching = **Motion**, not Waiting. Finding root causes = **Analyze**, not Measure.

sections.title: Ishikawa’s seven tools, fishbone and Pareto
sections.topic: Ishikawa’s Seven Tools, Fishbone and Pareto
points: **7 tools:** Fishbone (root causes by category) · Check sheet (collect data at source) · Histogram (shape of variation) · Pareto chart (vital few causes) · Control chart (signal vs noise over time) · Scatter diagram (test x→y) · Stratification (split by shift, region, product, release).
**Fishbone bones:** Methods, Machines/Tech, People, Materials/Data, Measurement, Environment. Find **root causes, not culprits**: ≥ 3 causes per bone, then circle 3 to test.

**Bank complaints Pareto (total 1,000):** refund delay 412, card declined 236, call-centre wait 158, incorrect charges 94, login/OTP 61, staff 24, statements 15. **Top 3 = 80.6%** → fix refund automation, card-decline rules and call routing first (Juran’s vital few vs useful many).

sections.title: Standards, maturity models, awards and digital quality
sections.topic: Standards, Maturity Models, Awards and Digital Quality
points: **CMMI levels:** 1 Initial · 2 Managed · 3 **Defined** (organisation-wide standard process) · 4 **Quantitatively managed** (statistically controlled) · 5 **Optimizing** (continuous improvement).
**ISO 9001:2015, 7 principles:** customer focus, leadership, engagement of people, process approach, improvement, evidence-based decisions, relationship management.
**Awards:** Deming Prize (Japan, 1951) · Malcolm Baldrige (US, 1987) · EFQM (Europe) · Tata Business Excellence Model (India, Baldrige-based) · CII-EXIM Bank Award (India).

**Digital quality:** shift left (tests, security and CI early); **DORA’s four keys** = deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore (speed and stability rise together); **SRE error budgets**: 99.9% monthly SLO ≈ 43 min downtime, and once the budget is spent you freeze features; **DORA 2024**: more AI adoption → 7.2% drop in delivery stability, and 39% report little or no trust in AI code.

sections.title: Cases: India and global, IT and non-IT
points: Each case asks one question: **was quality designed into the system, or bolted on?**

sections.title: Synthesis: seven ideas to carry out of the room
points: 1 **Choose your definition** (Garvin) · 2 **Fix the system, not the person** (Deming) · 3 **Prevention is cheapest** (Feigenbaum, Crosby) · 4 **Scale changes everything** (99.9% at 700M/day) · 5 **Culture beats toolkits** (Powell) · 6 **Quality and cost can move together** (Aravind, Narayana, Toyota) · 7 **Mind the exploration trap** (Benner & Tushman).
Exit ticket **3-2-1**: 3 concepts you could explain, 2 quality costs (P-A-I-E) you have seen, 1 open question or system to redesign.

decks.title: Vendor Management & Contracts
decks.subtitle: Make or buy, segment, select, contract, price, govern, exit · Session 7
decks.downloadName: Vendor Management and Contracts - Session 7 updated last class.pdf
decks.overview: You can outsource the work, never the accountability. Decide what not to buy (transaction-cost economics) and segment vendors (Kraljic). Select on total cost of ownership, not price. Read the liability clause first, let pricing models and SLAs do the managing, and plan the exit on day one.

sections.title: Why vendor management matters
points: **Opening poll, CrowdStrike–Delta (19 Jul 2024):** ~7,000 flights cancelled, ~1.3M customers, ~$500M loss. What can Delta recover? **Answer: C, low single-digit millions**, because the contract caps liability.

**Three numbers:** **9%** of annual value lost to poor contract management (WorldCC, 2020) · **1,050%** average annual support-price increase AT&T alleged after Broadcom bought VMware (2024) · **99%** of Toyota’s brake P-valves came from one supplier, Aisin, until a fire on 1 Feb 1997 (Nishiguchi & Beaudet, 1998).
Oracle–OpenAI: a **$300 billion** cloud deal, where most of Oracle’s new revenue comes from one customer. Vendor relationships are strategic.

sections.title: §1 Make, buy or ally: transaction-cost economics
points: **Three drivers (Williamson):** **asset specificity** (investments worth little outside the relationship), **uncertainty** (hard to specify, measure or foresee), **frequency** (how often it recurs). The higher they are, the more you move from market → hybrid → hierarchy.

**Market (buy):** spot purchases, catalogues, tenders: stationery, laptops, cabs; standard cloud storage; housekeeping, canteen. **Hybrid (ally):** long-term contracts, alliances, JVs: Maruti–supplier JVs, multi-year IT MSAs, P&G–JLL (Vested). **Hierarchy (make):** Toyota’s production know-how, a bank’s credit-risk models, Boeing buying back Spirit.

**Boeing–Spirit:** sold Wichita fuselage ops in 2005 → door plug Jan 2024 → re-acquired 8 Dec 2025 for **$8.3B EV, ~15,000 employees**. Fuselages are high asset-specificity, quality-critical work. Outsourcing the work didn’t outsource the accountability, and re-integration is the most expensive exit clause.
sections.tip: TCE takeaway: “keep what is **specific, uncertain and core**.”

sections.title: §2 Segment vendors: the Kraljic matrix
points: Axes: **profit impact** × **supply risk** (few suppliers, scarcity, switching cost). Kraljic (1983), HBR: “Purchasing must become supply management.”
Tip: **high spend ≠ strategic**. Ask how many credible suppliers could replace this one in 90 days.

sections.title: §3 Vendor selection and total cost of ownership
sections.topic: Vendor Selection and Total Cost of Ownership
points: **Dickson (1966):** 273 purchasing managers, 23 criteria. Top 8: Quality 3.51 · Delivery 3.42 · Performance history 3.00 · Warranties 2.85 · Production capacity 2.78 · **Price 2.76 (#6)** · Technical capability 2.55 · Financial position 2.51. **Weber, Current & Benton (1991):** 74 studies; price, delivery and quality are traded off together, especially under JIT.

**TCO = acquisition + ownership + exit.** Hidden costs include onboarding, integration, vendor-management staff, quality failures, downtime, renewal escalation and switching/exit (AT&T: $40–50M to leave VMware). Ellram (1995): firms that track TCO reward suppliers who reduce downstream costs.

**Six steps:** Define need → RFI → RFP/RFQ (same questions, scoring set in advance) → Evaluate (weighted scoring; L1 vs **QCBS**) → Due diligence → Negotiate & award (BATNA ready; contract before kick-off). GeM handled ₹5.4 lakh crore in FY 2024-25. **Winner’s curse:** a bid far below others returns as change requests.
**Hospital cloud exercise:** under the CFO’s weights **Y wins (7.95)**; under the CIO’s weights **Z wins (7.75)**. The weights decide the winner, so fix them before bids.

sections.title: §4 The contract: stack, clauses, liability, Indian law
sections.topic: The Contract Stack and Clauses that Bite
points: **Contract stack:** NDA/LOI → **MSA** (umbrella terms: liability, IP, data, termination, disputes; negotiated once) → **SOWs** (scope, deliverables, timeline, price, acceptance) → **Schedules** (SLAs, pricing, security, exit plan) → change requests. State the **order of precedence**. Example: Intelenet–Apria MSA (2009), ~120 pages, on SEC EDGAR.

**Ten clauses that bite:** scope · acceptance · change control · price & payment · service levels · warranties & indemnities · **limitation of liability** · data, security & IP · subcontracting & change of control · termination & exit.

**Liability anatomy:** **cap** (e.g. 12 months’ fees) · **exclusions** (indirect, consequential, lost profits) · **carve-outs, uncapped** (gross negligence, wilful misconduct, data/confidentiality breach, IP indemnity). Delta v. CrowdStrike: most claims dismissed (May 2025), but gross-negligence and computer-trespass claims proceed. Smart move: make vendor-caused regulatory fines **direct damages**.

**India toolkit:** Contract Act **s.73** (natural or foreseen loss only) · **s.74** (liquidated damages: reasonable compensation up to the stated sum) · Specific Relief Amendment 2018 (specific performance is the rule) · Arbitration Act 1996 (fix seat, rules, language, number of arbitrators) · **MSMED + s.43B(h)**: pay micro & small suppliers within **45 days (15 if no agreement)** · **DPDP 2023**: the fiduciary stays responsible for its processors.

sections.title: Negotiation: BATNA and ZOPA
points: **BATNA = Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement**, the “most important thing”. Steps: list alternatives → value each → pick the best (your BATNA) → set the lowest-valued deal you will accept.

**ZOPA** = the overlap between the seller’s settlement range (worst case → desired price) and the buyer’s (desired price → worst case). If the seller’s floor is above the buyer’s ceiling, **there is no ZOPA**.

**CIO scenario:** a $5M, 5-year contract → the vendor asks **$25M for 2 years** (“5-fold” in total, but **12.5× per year**). **Role-play:** buyer quoted 5× annual price; 1-year option at +7%; replacement takes ~18 months and ~2× a year’s fees; rival offers 6 months free. Vendor’s private floor is **2.5× for a 3-year commitment**.

sections.title: §5 Pricing models and SLAs that bite
points: **Risk line (buyer → vendor):** Time & materials / cost-plus → Fixed capacity → Fixed price / unit rate → Outcome / gain-share.

A good SLA states **metric, measurement method, target, window, exclusions, consequence**. **Service credits** are a capped % of monthly fees with earn-back. **Chronic failure** (Intelenet–Apria) = major credits in **3 consecutive months or 5 in 12** → termination right.
Avoid **watermelon SLAs** (green outside, red inside): pair them with experience measures (**XLAs**). Non-IT SLAs: OTIF (logistics), response & fix time (facilities), hygiene scores (catering).

sections.title: §6 Govern and exit: accountability stays with you
points: **Three tiers:** strategic (quarterly/annual, executive sponsors) · tactical (monthly service review) · operational (daily/weekly). Disputes climb **team → joint steering committee → executives → mediation/arbitration**. Quarterly scorecard: quality, delivery/SLA, cost & invoicing accuracy, responsiveness, risk & compliance, innovation. A red rating → action plan with an owner and a date.

**Regulation:** **RBI IT outsourcing (2023)**: the regulated entity stays accountable; audit and access rights; control sub-contracting; secure data at exit · **DPDP 2023 + Rules (Nov 2025)**: 18-month phase-in · **MeitY cloud MSA**: empanelled, audited providers; mandatory exit plan · **EU DORA (17 Jan 2025)**: register of ICT third-party contracts; direct oversight of critical providers.

**VMware–AT&T:** Broadcom’s ~$61B deal (Nov 2023) ended perpetual licences; AT&T sued 29 Aug 2024 (1,050% increase; 75,000 VMs on 8,600 servers; $40–50M to migrate); settled 22 Nov 2024. **Exit-proofing:** buyer-choice renewals with caps, change-of-control clause, termination assistance, open formats, source-code escrow, a tested exit plan, a credible second option.

sections.title: §7 Case clinic
points: Clinic steps: **Segment** (Kraljic before and after) → **Diagnose** (selection, contract, pricing, governance or exit?) → **Redraft** (the one clause that would have changed it) → **Recommend** (stay, renegotiate, dual-source or exit).

sections.title: Takeaways: six clauses to carry out of the room
points: §1 **Decide what not to buy** (keep what is specific, uncertain, core) · §2 **Segment, then negotiate** (Kraljic) · §3 **Select on total cost** (fix weights before bids; price the exit) · §4 **Read the liability clause first** · §5 **Make incentives do the work** (pricing and SLAs are management systems) · §6 **Plan the exit on day one**: you can outsource work, never accountability.

formulas.name: Weighted vendor score
formulas.expr: Score = Σ (weightᵢ × scoreᵢ), with Σ weights = 1

formulas.name: Total cost of ownership
formulas.example: Compare any renewal quote with the $40–50M switching cost

formulas.name: ZOPA
formulas.expr: ZOPA = [seller’s worst case, buyer’s worst case], if the seller’s floor ≤ the buyer’s ceiling
formulas.example: Seller $8M, buyer $11M → ZOPA $8M–$11M; seller $12M, buyer $10M → none

formulas.name: Annualised price change
